course_details.Overview of class: Modernity has dramatically changed the profile of Western Civilization and had a major impact on the European Jews. The course will take students from French Revolution that started integrating the Jews into the fabric of European society to the establishment of the State of Israel. It will highlight the plurality of models of Jewish integration and acculturation, the formation of new Jewish identities, the split of the traditional community under the impact of Haskalah (Jewish Enlightenment), the rise of Liberal and Orthodox trends within Judaism, and the spread of Jewish political movements such as socialism and nationalism. Based on a plethora of English-language documents, the course will introduce students to those problems of interaction between the general society and the Jewish minority that pointed toward the twentieth century transformation of modernity. In sum, the course will explore the fascinating response of Jews to modernity on political, societal, theological, and cultural levels.
course_details.Learning Objectives: • Acquire knowledge on the transformation of Jews from a marginalized and segregated diasporic ethno-religious group into an emancipated modern political nation, the process manifested in the political, philosophical, intellectual, economic, cultural and social contexts of major European and non-European empires (British, German, Russian, Austrian, Ottoman), colonial countries (Palestine, Northern Africa), and nation-states (Czechoslovakia, Poland, Lithuania, Turkey, Argentina) and considering the Jewish people top-down (Germany) and bottom-up (Italy, England, USA) forms of integration and acculturation in their specific socio-political contexts (e.g., late 18th century France, united post-1870s Germany, post-colonial Poland, socialist USSR) and organized thematically around key aspects of modernity (urbanization, emancipation, upward mobility, antisemitism, liberal arts, mass violence) through the in-depth investigation of verbal, visual, and auditory primary sources and by engaging the most updated secondary sources (historiography). • Develop critical skills including the framing of questions, delving into documentary analysis, and mastering contextualization; become acquainted with debates about models of Jewish integration and emancipation, balance the issues of grassroots and group agency and the role of political institutions of the state, evaluating historical evidence regarding the reasons for mass emigration to South Africa, Argentina, and the US, problematizing the established chronology of the Holocaust, and creating historical hypothesis to explain, e.g., the anti-imperial struggle of the Jews in Palestine for the establishment of the post-colonial state. • Appreciate the impact of political formulas (such as Abbe Gregoire statements on the Jews in National Assembly) on the forms and methods of Jewish social integration; acquire historical perspective on the rise of the scholarly study of Jews, Judaism, and Jewish civilization in the 19th century Germany and France; consider agency and subjectivity of Jews as a marginal group and marginal groups among the Jews (radical socialist youth, proletarian Zionists, financial tycoons, self-hating Jews, feminist Marxists, avant-gardist artists) and discuss ways to understand their choices and itineraries through a historical reconstruction; introduce the ways to modify grand historical narratives (e.g., "Jews left East Europe because of pogroms;" "Holocaust was planned in 1933," "all Bolsheviks were Jews") by using specific comparative contexts (e.g., ethnic minorities in the leftist movements) and analyzing newly discovered documents as one of the effective tools to reconstruct empiric reality and critically assess the ups and downs of modern historiography. • Problematize various forms of historical chronology (such as "the beginning of emancipation" or "the end of modernity"), explain regional and social differences in the processes of modernization, acculturation, and integration, and discuss various forms of counter-modernity (Jewish and non-Jewish) that complicate the conceptualization of "modern Jewish history." • Help students effectively to express the results of their research in written (response papers and a final paper), oral (class discussion, discussion groups) and visual forms (power-points, short in-class intervention on the basis of visual sources such as political posters and artwork), engage in a well-balanced debate with creators of newest historical narratives, and analyze hidden and explicit agendas, rhetorical tools, and audience of the historical documents of the past.

course_info.course_name: Fossil Fuels and Climate Change in Palestine/Israe

course_details.Instructors:
Shira Pinhas
Crowe 5-167
Office Hours: Wednesdays 10:00 – 12:00
Shira Pinhas is a Weinberg College Postdoctoral Fellow in Jewish Studies. She is a historian of the social and material history of Palestine/Israel and the broader Levant region. Her research focuses on understanding how new infrastructures and technologies, along with transnational flows of energy, materials, capital, and labor, shaped political hierarchies and social subjectivities during the twentieth century. Before joining Northwestern, Pinhas was a Postdoctoral Research Fellow and Lecturer at Princeton University’s Institute for the Transregional Study of the Contemporary Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia, and a Polonsky Postdoctoral Fellow at the Van Leer Jerusalem Institute. She received her PhD from Tel Aviv University in 2023.
course_details.Overview of class: "Guns don't kill people, people kill people" (American proverb). "You are different with a gun in your hand; the gun is different with you holding it" (Bruno Latour, Pandora's Hope: Essays on the Reality of Science Studies, 179). These two sayings present diametrically opposed views of the relationship between weapons and society: one regards weapons as a neutral medium that merely executes violent human intentions, while the other attributes to them agency in shaping those very intentions. This course examines this tension through the history of violence and arms in Palestine/Israel, spanning the periods of the Ottoman Empire, British rule, and the establishment of the State of Israel up to the present day. Violence is a human experience unlike any other. It leaves deep emotional and physical imprints, and sometimes transforms the very way people perceive and sense the world. To examine this, we will engage with poetry, music, and film alongside archival sources, inquiring into how violence has shaped the subjectivities of perpetrators, victims, witnesses, and bystanders across various times and contexts. Can violence form a collective identity or experience? Rather than considering these questions abstractly, we will situate them in the material realities of technology. We will analyze how changing forms of surveillance, policing, and bombing have shaped ideas of humanity, delineating who belongs to it and who is excluded from it. Throughout the course, we will ask: What made different people at different points in time decide to use arms or object to their use? How and to what extent did the materiality of arms - their production, dissemination, design, or operation - influence these choices?
course_details.Learning Objectives: The course is designed with three key objectives in mind: to explore how arms shaped and were shaped by the social and cultural history of Palestine/Israel; to examine diverse perspectives on arms production and use as experienced and enacted by various historical actors; and, perhaps most crucially, to analyze how militarization has profoundly shaped the subjectivities of those affected by it across different times and contexts. To achieve these insights, a central aim of the seminar is to guide students in analyzing historical sources, contextualizing them, and constructing well-founded arguments based on their analyses.

course_details.Overview of class: With a warming rate double the global average and half of the world's oil reserves, the Middle East is a pivotal site for understanding the history, present, and future of climate change. Although Israel/Palestine is not today an oil-producing country, historically it was imagined differently: in the 19th and 20th centuries it was considered a promising frontier for oil exploration and became a regional hub of fossil fuel infrastructures, channeling Middle Eastern oil and North African gas to Europe. This seminar examines how the rise of fossil fuels and the dynamics of climate change played out in Palestine/Israel and shaped both the Zionist-Palestinian struggle and Palestine's place within the Middle East. We will consider how the Middle East became "Middle" through the interplay between energy sources, infrastructures, and colonial powers. We will explore how carbonization in the region gave rise to new forms of political rule, reshaping identities and altering environments, and how seemingly mundane infrastructures - from coaling depots to automobility - enabled and managed colonial power as well as resistance to it. Drawing on archival materials alongside fiction, poetry, and film in Arabic and Hebrew (all provided in English translation), we will analyze the intimate, everyday, and affective dimensions of carbonization and warming, exploring how these forces shaped subjectivities and societies. Finally, we will consider how different notions of heat and cooling technologies were tied to specific constructions of gender, race, and class.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Debunk common myths about energy transitions; Understand the historical complexities of the transition to fossil fuels and climate change; Debunk common myths about oil in the Middle East; Understand how different historical actors experienced and understood carbonization and warming.

course_details.Overview of class: The 19th and 20th centuries witnessed a profound transformation of Jewish life in almost every facet. What changes when we look at modern Jewish history through the lenses of gender and sexuality? This course explores the major themes in Jewish history of the Modern era - emancipation, assimilation, and modernization itself - with a focus on the impact of ideas and experiences of gender and sexuality. We will follow the changing relationships of Jews to the societies of which they formed an integral part, with a focus on the European and Ottoman empires, the nation states that came to replace them, and the United States. Throughout this historical progression, the class will showcase how ideas about normative masculinity and femininity defined how Jews experienced and made sense of the historical forces they faced: secularization and religious revival, acculturation, immigration, racism, and nationalism.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Identify and analyze key themes in modern Jewish history, using gender as a useful category of historical analysis. Compare Jewish experiences of modernity across European, Ottoman, and American contexts. Examine and interpret primary sources and historical scholarship through close and comparative reading. Develop writing, collaboration, and interpersonal communication skills.

course_details.Overview of class: The Talmud is one of the most important works of Jewish literature. For the last millennium, Talmud study has been a central part of Jewish religious and cultural practice. Despite the splintering of Judaism into different denominations, Jews the world over are unified by their commitment to studying Talmud. The Talmud is an unusual work of literature, and it has been credited as an influence on codes of law, sermons, modern works of Jewish literature, and even Seinfeld. This course will explain the Talmud's import and durability within Jewish culture while introducing students to the rigors of legal analysis that lie at the heart of most talmudic passages. The course is ideal for those interested in religion, law, logic games and questions of textual interpretation. The course will study the Talmud entirely in English translation; there is neither a language prerequisite nor an expectation of prior experience reading the Talmud. The course counts toward Religion, Law and Politics (RLP) religious studies major concentration.
course_details.Learning Objectives: • Reading and comprehending any passage of the Talmud (in translation). • Ancient Jewish history • Overview of Jewish ideas • Thinking like a lawyer • Critical reading

Zavier Nunn is a historian of modern Europe whose work focuses on medical and legal efforts to regulate sex—who may engage in it, who may change it, and how—alongside the lived experiences of those subject to social and state policing.
course_details.Overview of class: Sex and Nazi Germany: two charged topics. What do they have to do with each other? More than you might think. The Nazis cared a great deal about sex. Decisions about who should have children, and who should be sterilized, sat at the center of racial policy. Brothels were set up for soldiers and for forced laborers in concentration camps. Paragraph 175 sent thousands of gay men to prison and then to the camps as well. At the same time, ordinary Germans were promised pleasure, a right extended to "Aryans" and withheld from Jews and other "undesirables." Sex had a purpose for the Third Reich: it fed the birth rate, enforced labor discipline, lifted military morale, and fueled racial war. Racism, Dagmar Herzog writes, has always also been about sex. Under National Socialism this was true in the extreme. Studying who could have sex—or change sex—and how in the Third Reich tells us as much about racial purity, biopolitics, national identity, and state policy, as sex itself. We will cover the sexual cultures of Weimar Berlin, Nazi reproductive and racial policy, the homoerotics of fascist masculinity, Nazi theories of sexuality, the persecution of gay men, lesbians, and transvestites, sexual violence in the camps, and the place of sex in the cultural memory of Nazi Germany. Students will encounter this history through court records, medical files, memoirs, photographs, film, and scholarship.
course_details.Learning Objectives: Students will develop a comprehensive understanding of how the Nazi state mobilized sex, gender, and sexuality to police inclusion and exclusion within German society. The course examines specific manifestations of sexual policing and incitement through law, medicine, culture, and media. By the end of the quarter, students will be able to identify how sexuality and gender operated within Nazi society—both among marginalized populations and those prioritized by the regime—and articulate informed interpretations of their historical significance. However, the learning objectives extend beyond knowledge acquisition. I am invested in cultivating broadly applicable skills: deep and close reading, critical thinking, primary-source analysis and information extraction, and the clear, sophisticated articulation of ideas and arguments in both oral and written form. These skills will be practiced in the classroom and further honed through assessment. My hope is that students will carry these skills forward as lifelong tools for navigating the complexities of the present and the future.

course_details.Overview of class:
Title: Jews in Iran
Iran is home to one of the oldest, and currently, the largest Jewish communities in the Middle East outside of Isreal. This course follows Jewish Iranian history from the 7th century to the present introducing students more broadly to the history of Iran and the historical role that religious minorities played in Iranian and Middle Eastern histories. We will situate the stories of Iranian Jews in comparison to that of other Jewish communities in the Middle East. We will focus on questions of identity, assimilation, and historical agency: To what extent were Jews integrated into their Persian speaking environment? How did Jews shape Iranian history? And how does the Jewish community of Iran endure to this day while other lively Jewish communities in Iraq, Yemen, Morocco, and Egypt emigrated elsewhere?
course_details.Learning Objectives: -Students will become familiar with key themes related to the history of Iranian Jews, and the relevant primary sources. - Develop skills of historical analysis using secondary and primary sources including texts, images, objects, maps, and more. This includes the ability the evaluate accounts in their historical context and assessing current scholarly discussions and debates in the history of Iran and religious minorities in the Middle East. - Consider broader historical social contexts and structures. - We will work on our transferable skillset: critical thinking and reading, argumentation and debate, and structured, evidence supported writing.
